questions.question: What does a monoid add to the structure of a semigroup?
options: A determinant.
An identity element.
An inner product.
A requirement that every element has an inverse.
questions.explanation: A semigroup already has a closed associative binary operation; a monoid is a semigroup that additionally contains a two-sided identity.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: a monoid is a semigroup with a neutral element.

questions.skill_detail: Distinguish monoids from semigroups.
option_explanations: A determinant is a matrix invariant and is not part of the abstract monoid axioms.
An inner product is extra vector-space geometry, not a monoid requirement.
Requiring every element to have an inverse upgrades a monoid to a group.

options: Yes, but only if the operation is addition.
Yes. Every monoid is automatically a group.
No. That extra condition leads toward groups.
No, because monoids cannot have identity elements.
questions.explanation: A monoid requires associativity and an identity but not inverses for all elements; adding universal inverses produces a group.

questions.skill_detail: Separate monoids from groups.
option_explanations: The absence of an inverse requirement is independent of whether the operation is addition.
Monoids such as $\mathbb N_0$ under addition contain elements without inverses, so not every monoid is a group.
An identity is required for every monoid, so this proposed reason states the opposite axiom.

questions.question: Why is every group automatically a monoid?
options: A group has an associative operation and an identity element.
A group has no binary operation
A group has no inverse elements.
A group operation is not closed, which is false
questions.explanation: Every group has a closed associative binary operation, an identity, and inverses; the first two structural properties plus identity already satisfy all monoid axioms.

questions.question: What role does the identity element play in a monoid?
options: It swaps the order of multiplication.
It makes every product equal to zero.
It is a neutral element for the operation.
It replaces associativity.
questions.explanation: The monoid identity $e$ is neutral on both sides: $e\star a=a\star e=a$ for every element $a$.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: a monoid is a semigroup with a neutral element.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Interpret the identity in a monoid.
option_explanations: Swapping factors is commutativity and is not performed by the identity element.
A neutral element preserves each input rather than making every result zero.
Associativity remains a separate monoid axiom and cannot be replaced by an identity.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

No, because monoids are not associative.
Yes. Every monoid is Abelian.
Only if the set is finite.
questions.explanation: Commutativity is optional for a monoid; for example, square matrices under multiplication form a generally noncommutative monoid.

Finiteness does not determine commutativity; finite monoids can be commutative or noncommutative.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb N_0,+)$ a monoid?
options: Addition is associative and $0$ is an identity element.
Addition is not closed on $\mathbb N_0$.
Every natural number has an additive inverse in $\mathbb N_0$.
The identity element is $1$.
questions.explanation: Addition maps nonnegative integers to nonnegative integers, is associative, and has $0$ as a two-sided identity, so $(\mathbb N_0,+)$ is a monoid.
questions.source_support: Examples: $(\mathbb N,+)$ is a monoid with identity $0$ when $0$ is included.

Positive elements lack additive inverses in $\mathbb N_0$, but inverses are not required for a monoid.
Under addition, $1$ is not neutral because $a+1\ne a$; the identity is $0$.

The additive identity $0$ is not in the set.
Every positive integer has an inverse.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb N,+)$ a monoid?
options: Addition is associative and closed, and $0$ is an identity
Every natural number has an additive inverse in $\mathbb N$
$1$ is the identity because $n+1=n$
Addition is commutative, and commutativity alone defines a monoid
questions.explanation: Natural-number addition is a closed associative binary operation, and $0+n=n+0=n$. These are exactly the semigroup and identity requirements for a monoid.
questions.source_support: The course gives $(\mathbb N,+)$ as a monoid with identity $0$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Check associativity and the identity in the course monoid example.
option_explanations: For $n>0$, $-n\notin\mathbb N$, so additive inverses are absent. A monoid does not require inverses; adding that requirement would describe a group.
$n+1\ne n$ for natural numbers, so $1$ is not the additive identity. The common misread is to transfer the multiplicative identity to addition.
Commutativity is not the defining condition for a monoid. The required conditions are associativity and an identity element for the stated binary operation.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: For $n\times n$ matrices under multiplication, what is the monoid identity?
options: The matrix with all diagonal entries zero.
$I_n$
The zero matrix.
Any invertible matrix.
questions.explanation: The identity matrix satisfies $I_nA=AI_n=A$ for every $n\times n$ matrix, so it is the monoid identity.
questions.source_support: Definition: identity element leaves every element unchanged.

questions.skill_detail: Identify the identity in a matrix monoid.
option_explanations: A matrix with zero diagonal entries cannot preserve arbitrary matrices under multiplication.
The zero matrix absorbs multiplication, $0A=A0=0$, rather than leaving $A$ unchanged.
An arbitrary invertible matrix changes most factors; only $I_n$ is neutral for every $A$.

questions.question: On $\{0,1,2\}$ with operation $\max$, which element is the identity?
options: There is no identity.
questions.explanation: For $a\in\{0,1,2\}$, $\max(0,a)=a=\max(a,0)$, so the minimum element $0$ is the identity.
questions.source_support: Definition: a monoid has an identity element.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
questions.skill_detail: Find identity in a max monoid.
option_explanations: Using $1$ changes $0$ to $1$, since $\max(1,0)=1\ne0$.
Using $2$ sends every input to $2$, so it is absorbing rather than neutral.
The element $0$ satisfies both identity equations, so an identity does exist.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: What can prevent a semigroup from being a monoid?
options: The absence of an identity element in the set.
The existence of a binary operation.
The presence of associativity.
The presence of closure.
questions.explanation: A semigroup already has closure and associativity; it fails to be a monoid precisely when no two-sided identity lies in the set.
questions.source_support: Interpretation: monoid is a semigroup with a neutral element.

option_explanations: A binary operation is required for a semigroup and therefore cannot obstruct monoid status.
Associativity is shared by semigroups and monoids, so its presence moves in the right direction.
Closure is also required by both structures and cannot be the missing condition.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Is $(\mathbb N_0,\times)$ a monoid?
options: Yes, with identity $1$.
No, because $1$ is not in $\mathbb N_0$.
No, because $0$ has no inverse.
No, because multiplication is not associative.
questions.explanation: Nonnegative integers are closed under associative multiplication, and $1a=a1=a$, so $(\mathbb N_0,\times)$ is a monoid with identity $1$.

questions.question: Is the set of all invertible $2\times2$ matrices under multiplication a monoid?

No, because $I_2$ is not invertible.

Only if all matrices commute.
questions.explanation: Invertible $2\times2$ matrices are closed under associative multiplication and include invertible identity $I_2$, so they form a monoid (indeed a group).

The identity satisfies $I_2^{-1}=I_2$, so it is invertible.

questions.question: For $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb Z$, what is the identity element showing that this is a monoid?
options: No identity exists.
questions.explanation: An identity $e$ must satisfy $a\star e=a+e+1=a$, which gives $e=-1$; the same value also satisfies $e\star a=a$.

Solving the identity equation explicitly produces $-1$, so an identity does exist.
